## Self-Refine and Reflexion

Two foundational approaches to iterative LLM quality improvement:

| Approach | Mechanism | Key Result | Source |
|----------|-----------|------------|--------|
| Self-Refine [1] | Generate, self-feedback, refine | ~20% absolute improvement across 7 tasks | [1] |
| Reflexion [2] | Verbal reflection into episodic memory | 91% pass@1 on HumanEval (vs 80% GPT-4 baseline) | [2] |

**Self-Refine** requires no supervised training, RL, or additional data — the same model generates, critiques, and refines its own output [1]. The ~20% improvement spans tasks from dialog generation to mathematical reasoning [1].

**Reflexion** stores verbal reflections in a memory buffer for use in subsequent trials [2]. The mechanism is: receive feedback, verbal reflection, store in memory, use in next attempt [2]. No model weight updates are needed [2].

> Note: Reflexion's abstract does not explicitly name an "Actor/Evaluator/Self-Reflection" architecture — the mechanism is feedback-reflection-memory [2].

## CriticGPT

OpenAI's CriticGPT [4] provides the strongest evidence for LLM-based code quality evaluation:

| Metric | Value | Condition |
|--------|-------|-----------|
| Preference for model critiques over human | **63%** | Naturally occurring LLM errors |
| Errors found in "flawless" training data | Hundreds | ChatGPT training data |
| False bug risk | Present | Critics can hallucinate bugs |

> "On naturally occurring LLM errors, model-written critiques preferred over human critiques in 63% of cases" [4]

Human-machine teams catch similar numbers of bugs to LLM critics alone while hallucinating less [4]. This suggests the optimal configuration is human-LLM collaboration, not pure LLM evaluation.

## LLM-as-Judge

Gu et al.'s survey [7] covers the reliability of LLM-as-Judge systems with strategies for improving consistency and mitigating biases. The survey spans diverse domains and complex tasks [7].

**Limitation:** The abstract does not specifically address code quality evaluation [7]. Code-specific LLM-as-Judge patterns are not enumerated in the accessible content.

The evaluator-optimizer pattern from Anthropic [11] formalizes this:

> "One LLM generates, another evaluates in a loop. Effective when clear evaluation criteria exist and iterative refinement measurably improves outcomes." [11]

## Evaluator-Optimizer Pattern (Anthropic)

Anthropic's six agentic patterns [11] include evaluator-optimizer as a core architecture:

| Pattern | Description | Code Quality Application |
|---------|-------------|------------------------|
| Evaluator-Optimizer | Generate + evaluate in loop | Iterative code refinement |
| Orchestrator-Workers | Central LLM delegates to specialized workers | "Suited for unpredictable subtask requirements, such as coding tasks affecting multiple files" [11] |
| Parallelization (Voting) | Same task, diverse outputs | Best-of-N code generation |

**CORRECTION:** No "90.2% improvement" figure appears anywhere in the Effective Agents article [11]. Any citation of this figure to Anthropic is unsubstantiated.

## Aider Architect/Editor Pattern

Aider's architect mode [24] implements a two-model pattern where one model (architect) plans changes and another (editor) implements them. This separates quality reasoning from code production — the architect can evaluate and refine the plan before committing to implementation.

**Access:** Snippet-level only; full page not fetched [24].

## AI Code Review Tools

| Tool | Model | Configuration | Source |
|------|-------|---------------|--------|
| CodeRabbit [26] | Multiple LLMs | YAML-based rule configuration | [26] |
| Qodo Merge [25] | Multiple LLMs | Configurable review rules | [25] |
| SonarQube AI Code Assurance [37] | Integrated | Quality gate integration | [37] |

CodeRabbit's own analysis of 470 PRs found AI-authored code has 10.83 issues/PR vs 6.45 for human code [17] — a 1.7x ratio. Category breakdowns [17]:

| Issue Category | AI vs Human Ratio |
|----------------|-------------------|
| Logic/correctness errors | 1.75x |
| Readability issues | >3x |
| Error handling gaps | ~2x |
| Security issues | up to 2.74x |
| Formatting problems | 2.66x |
| Naming inconsistencies | ~2x |

Caveat: CodeRabbit is a vendor in this space — the study is self-commissioned [17]. Authorship attribution methodology: "Since it was impossible to directly confirm authorship of each PR of a large enough OSS dataset, we checked for signals that a PR was co-authored by AI" [17].

## YAGNI and Proportionality

Addy Osmani [36] provides practitioner guidance on YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It) considerations in AI coding workflows. Not fetched for full verification.

The broader principle: LLM-generated code tends toward over-engineering — adding capabilities, abstractions, and patterns that are not needed for the immediate requirement. Quality evaluation must include necessity assessment, not just correctness.

Sun et al. frame this as a misalignment: "a misalignment between academic focus, industry priorities, and observed model behavior" [8] — academics focus on correctness metrics while practitioners prioritize maintainability [8].

## Harness-Based Quality Evaluation

Fowler's harness engineering framework [15] categorizes quality evaluation as:

| Type | Speed | Determinism | Examples |
|------|-------|-------------|----------|
| Computational sensors | ms-seconds | Deterministic | Tests, linters, type checkers |
| Inferential sensors | Slower | Non-deterministic | Code review agents, LLM-as-judge |

> "Separately, you get either an agent that keeps repeating the same mistakes (feedback-only) or an agent that encodes rules but never finds out whether they worked." [15]

This argues for combining both: computational checks for objective criteria and inferential evaluation for subjective quality.

## Quality Frameworks

Sun et al. [8] apply ISO/IEC 25010 to LLM-generated code quality:

> "the need to integrate quality assurance mechanisms into LLM code generation pipelines to ensure that future generated code not only passes tests but truly passes with quality" [8]

Their 109-paper literature review + industry workshops + empirical analysis of 3 LLMs represents the most comprehensive quality framework study in this space [8].

Zietsman's three hypotheses [10] add that correlated errors in homogeneous LLM pipelines "echo rather than cancel" — using the same model family for generation and review may miss systematic blind spots [10].

## Gaps and Limitations

- CriticGPT 63% figure is for naturally occurring errors only — no higher figure confirmed from abstract [4]
- LLM-as-Judge survey [7] does not specifically cover code quality in accessible content
- Aider architect mode [24], Qodo Merge [25], CodeRabbit config [26], SonarQube [37] were not fetched for detailed verification
- CodeRabbit quality study is vendor-commissioned with uncertain authorship attribution [17]
- No controlled study comparing evaluator-optimizer loop code quality vs single-pass generation
- YAGNI quantification is absent — the problem is widely acknowledged but not measured
- Zietsman's planted-bug methodology is "directional evidence, not a controlled demonstration" [10]
- Self-Refine task-specific results for code optimization not extractable from abstract alone [1]
